title: Key Health and Safety Legislation and the Role of the HSE
exam_alert: Know the difference: an Improvement Notice allows time to fix a problem; a Prohibition Notice stops the activity immediately. The test often asks which notice applies to an immediate danger.
common_mistake: Many candidates assume HSE only gets involved after an accident has happened. In reality, inspectors can visit and act on any site at any time, accident or not.
memory_aid: P for Prohibition = Pause the work immediately. I for Improvement = Interval to fix it.

quick_check.q: What is the key difference between an Improvement Notice and a Prohibition Notice?
quick_check.a: An Improvement Notice allows a set period of time to fix the problem; a Prohibition Notice stops the dangerous activity immediately.

how_tested: questions here usually ask you to name the correct Act, or to identify what an HSE inspector is legally able to do --- not just what they typically do.

title: Employer and Worker Duties and Responsibilities
exam_alert: Responsibility is shared, not one-directional. The test frequently checks whether you know workers carry personal legal duties too, not just employers.
common_mistake: "Reasonably practicable" is often misread as "whatever is cheapest or easiest." It actually means weighing the level of risk against the cost and effort of controlling it --- a higher risk justifies a higher cost to control.
memory_aid: Section 2 = Employer's duty to protect. Section 7 = Your (worker's) duty to take care. Section 8 = Don't interfere or misuse.
how_tested: scenario questions here often test whether you understand that duty is shared --- expect questions asking whose responsibility a specific failure is, not just what the law generally requires.

title: Site Management Structure, Policies, and Site Rules
exam_alert: A Principal Contractor is only required when more than one contractor is involved on the project --- a common trap in scenario questions.
common_mistake: Candidates often confuse the Principal Designer (responsible before construction starts, during design) with the Principal Contractor (responsible once construction is underway).
memory_aid: Designer plans it on paper first; Contractor builds it on site second --- their CDM duties follow the same order.

quick_check.q: When is a Principal Contractor required on a construction project under CDM 2015?
quick_check.a: Whenever more than one contractor is involved on the project.

how_tested: expect questions asking which duty holder is responsible for a specific task, particularly distinguishing the Principal Designer's pre-construction role from the Principal Contractor's on-site role.

title: Inductions, Toolbox Talks, and Permits to Work
exam_alert: A permit to work is an additional, time-specific control --- it does not replace the risk assessment and method statement for the task.
common_mistake: Toolbox talks are sometimes treated as informal and unrecorded. They should be logged, since they form part of a worker's ongoing training record.
memory_aid: Induction = once, at the start. Toolbox talk = often, along the way. Permit to work = every time, for the highest-risk tasks.
how_tested: questions often test whether you can tell a permit-to-work situation apart from one that only needs a standard risk assessment and method statement.

title: Record-Keeping and Consequences of Non-Compliance
exam_alert: Appealing a Prohibition Notice does not suspend it --- work stays stopped throughout the appeal. An appealed Improvement Notice is suspended until the appeal is decided.
common_mistake: Candidates often assume only the company can be prosecuted. Individual directors and managers can be personally prosecuted under Section 37 of HASAWA.
memory_aid: No record = no proof it happened. To an inspector, an undocumented risk assessment is treated the same as one that was never done.

quick_check.q: Does appealing a Prohibition Notice pause its effect while the appeal is being decided?
quick_check.a: No --- unlike an Improvement Notice, a Prohibition Notice stays in effect throughout the appeal.

how_tested: expect questions matching a described failure to its likely consequence, and questions testing whether appealing a notice pauses it.

title: Principles of Risk Assessment
exam_alert: The five steps are tested in order more often than you'd expect: Identify, Decide who's harmed, Evaluate and decide precautions, Record and implement, Review. Losing track of the order is an easy way to drop marks.
common_mistake: Candidates often treat risk assessment as a one-time paperwork exercise completed before work starts. In reality, the final step --- review --- continues for as long as the task does.
memory_aid: "I Dress Each Risk Right": Identify, Decide who's harmed, Evaluate and precautions, Record, Review.

quick_check.q: What is the final step of the HSE's five steps to risk assessment, and why does it matter?
quick_check.a: Review --- because conditions on site change, and an assessment that isn't reviewed and updated no longer reflects the actual risk.

how_tested: the test often asks you to put the five steps in the correct order, or to identify which step is missing from a described scenario.

title: Identifying Hazards on Site
exam_alert: Hazard and risk are not the same thing: the hazard is the thing that could cause harm; the risk is the chance of that harm actually happening and how bad it would be.
common_mistake: Candidates often focus only on obvious physical hazards and overlook categories like noise, dust, or manual handling strain, which are just as commonly tested.
memory_aid: Hazard = what could hurt you. Risk = how likely, and how badly.
how_tested: questions frequently present a scenario and ask you to identify which element is the hazard and which is the risk --- don't assume the terms are interchangeable.

title: Method Statements and Safe Systems of Work
exam_alert: A method statement that is generic or reused across different jobs does not meet the legal standard --- it must be specific to the actual task and site.
common_mistake: Many assume that once RAMS is signed off, it doesn't need to change. It must be reviewed and updated if the task or site conditions change partway through.
memory_aid: Risk Assessment finds the danger. Method Statement explains, step by step, how the work avoids it.

quick_check.q: What is RAMS, and why must it be specific to the task rather than reused from a similar job?
quick_check.a: RAMS combines the Risk Assessment and Method Statement into one document; it must be task-specific because a generic document doesn't reflect the actual hazards and conditions of the job being done.

how_tested: expect questions asking what a method statement should contain, or testing whether you know it must be updated when conditions change, not treated as fixed once signed off.

title: Hierarchy of Control Measures
exam_alert: When a question lists several valid control measures, the correct answer is usually the one highest up the hierarchy, not just any option that would technically work.
common_mistake: PPE is often chosen first because it's the most familiar control measure. It is actually the last resort, used once higher-level controls aren't fully sufficient on their own.
memory_aid: E-S-E-C-P: Eliminate, Substitute, Engineering, Control (admin), PPE --- from most to least effective.

quick_check.q: Why does a secured guardrail protect workers more reliably than a safety harness alone?
quick_check.a: A guardrail is an engineering control that protects everyone near it without depending on correct use; a harness is PPE, which only protects the wearer and only if it's used correctly every time.

how_tested: the test often asks which control measure should be used first, or gives a list of measures and asks you to identify the most effective one --- not simply a correct one.

title: Worker Involvement in Risk Assessment
exam_alert: Don't assume risk assessment is a one-directional process from manager to worker. Workers have a legal right to be consulted, and a duty to report hazards as they're spotted.
common_mistake: Some candidates assume a risk assessment can't be questioned once work has started. A worker who spots a new hazard is expected to report it, triggering a review.
memory_aid: The risk assessment doesn't end when the paperwork is signed --- it ends when the task does.

quick_check.q: If a worker spots a new hazard partway through a task that wasn't in the original risk assessment, what should happen?
quick_check.a: The hazard should be reported immediately, and the risk assessment reviewed and updated before work continues.

how_tested: questions here often test whether you understand that workers have both a right to be consulted and an active duty to report, not just a passive duty to follow instructions.

title: Types of Accidents, Incidents, and RIDDOR Reporting
exam_alert: Specified injuries and dangerous occurrences: report without delay. Over-7-day injuries: report within 15 days. These two timescales are the ones most often swapped by mistake.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes assume RIDDOR only covers fatalities. It also covers specified injuries, over-7-day injuries, dangerous occurrences, and occupational diseases.
memory_aid: Serious and Sudden = Speedy (without delay). Seven days off = Fifteen days to report.

quick_check.q: Within how many days of the accident must an over-7-day injury be reported under RIDDOR?
quick_check.a: 15 days.

how_tested: the test frequently asks which timescale applies to which category --- without delay, 10 days, or 15 days --- so the categories and their deadlines need to be kept straight, not just the fact that reporting is required.

title: Near Misses, Unsafe Conditions, and First Aid Provision
exam_alert: There is no single fixed number of first aiders required by law --- provision must match what the site's own risk assessment identifies as necessary.
common_mistake: Some candidates assume a near miss doesn't need reporting because no one was hurt. It should be reported for exactly the same reason an accident is --- to fix the gap before it does cause harm.
memory_aid: A near miss is a warning you got to hear without having to be the one it happened to.
how_tested: expect questions testing whether you know first aid provision is risk-assessed and site-specific, not a single fixed legal number applied everywhere.

title: Causes and Prevention of Fire on Site
exam_alert: Removing just one side of the fire triangle --- heat, fuel, or oxygen --- is enough to prevent or stop a fire. You don't need to remove all three.
common_mistake: Hot work gets most of the attention, but electrical faults and poorly stored flammable materials cause just as many site fires, and are tested just as often.
memory_aid: Heat, Fuel, Oxygen --- break one side of the triangle, and the fire collapses.

quick_check.q: What are the three elements of the fire triangle, and how many need to be removed to stop a fire?
quick_check.a: Heat, fuel, and oxygen --- removing just one of the three is enough to prevent or extinguish a fire.

how_tested: questions here often test whether you can name all three elements of the fire triangle, or identify a prevention measure that addresses a specific cause.

title: Fire Detection, Alarms, and Firefighting Equipment
exam_alert: A water extinguisher (red label) must never be used on an electrical fire --- one of the most consistently tested facts in this subchapter.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes assume any extinguisher will do in an emergency. The type must match the class of fire, or it can make the situation more dangerous, not less.
memory_aid: Red for ordinary materials, Cream for liquids too, Black for electrics --- keep well clear, Blue for powder, the all-rounder, Yellow for the chip-pan fryer.
how_tested: expect questions matching an extinguisher's colour or type to the correct fire, and questions testing which type must never be used on an electrical fire.

title: Emergency Evacuation Procedures and Assembly Points
exam_alert: Never return to a building or work area during an evacuation to collect belongings or finish a task --- the test treats this as an automatic wrong answer in any scenario question.
common_mistake: The head count at the assembly point is sometimes seen as a formality. It's actually what tells the emergency services whether someone is still unaccounted for inside.
memory_aid: Alarm sounds, tools down, straight to the assembly point --- no exceptions, no detours.

quick_check.q: What is the first thing a worker should do when the fire alarm sounds?
quick_check.a: Stop work immediately and make their way via the nearest safe route to the designated assembly point.

how_tested: the test commonly checks whether you know evacuation is immediate and unconditional, and why the head count at the assembly point matters.

title: COSHH and Hazardous Substances
exam_alert: COSHH applies to hazardous dust and fumes generated by a task --- such as from cutting or grinding --- just as much as it applies to chemical products brought onto site.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes think COSHH only concerns chemicals with a warning label on the container. Dust, fumes, and vapours produced by the work itself are covered just as fully.
memory_aid: If it could get into your lungs, onto your skin, or into your eyes while you work --- COSHH applies, whatever its source.

quick_check.q: Does COSHH only apply to chemical products brought onto site, or also to substances created by the work itself?
quick_check.a: Both --- COSHH covers dust, fumes, and vapours generated by the task, not only products that arrive in a labelled container.

how_tested: questions here often test whether you know COSHH covers substances created by the work itself, such as cutting dust, not just products that arrive in a labelled container.

title: Asbestos and Silica Dust Awareness
exam_alert: Never assume a material is safe just because it looks fine. If there's any doubt about asbestos, the only correct response is to stop, avoid disturbing it further, and report it.
common_mistake: Some candidates think a standard dust mask is enough protection against silica dust. Water suppression or on-tool extraction must be used first, with RPE as an additional control, not the only one.
memory_aid: Asbestos: if in doubt, don't. Silica: suppress it before you breathe it.

quick_check.q: What is the workplace exposure limit for respirable crystalline silica?
quick_check.a: 0.1 mg/m³ as an 8-hour time-weighted average.

how_tested: expect questions testing the correct response to suspected asbestos, and recall of the exact silica exposure limit figure.

title: Safe Storage, Handling, and Respiratory Protection
exam_alert: Facial hair at the seal line of tight-fitting RPE breaks the seal and compromises protection --- regardless of the mask's filter rating.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes assume any dust mask provides adequate protection. The filter class must match the hazard --- FFP3 for fine, hazardous dust, not a basic FFP1 nuisance-dust mask.
memory_aid: The right mask, wrongly fitted, protects no one. Rating and seal both have to be right.
how_tested: questions often test whether you understand that a mask's protection depends on both its filter rating and a properly fitted seal --- one without the other isn't enough.

title: Noise and Vibration Hazards
exam_alert: 87 dB(A) is the exposure limit value that must never be exceeded --- even with hearing protection factored in. It is frequently confused with the lower 80 and 85 dB(A) action values.
common_mistake: Some candidates assume hearing protection is only needed once noise feels uncomfortable. It is a legal requirement at specific measured action values, not a matter of personal judgement.
memory_aid: Noise: 80 offer, 85 must wear, 87 never exceed. Vibration: 2.5 act, 5.0 is the limit --- for the hands; half those values for the whole body.
how_tested: the test often asks for the exact dB or vibration figures at each threshold, and what action is required once each one is reached.

title: Manual Handling Principles, Risk Assessment, and Mechanical Aids
exam_alert: There is no single legal maximum weight for manual lifting. The TILE assessment --- Task, Individual, Load, Environment --- is what determines what's safe for that specific situation.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes assume a fixed weight figure makes a lift automatically safe or unsafe. The same weight can be safe or dangerous depending on the task, the person, the load's stability, and the environment.
memory_aid: TILE: Task, Individual, Load, Environment --- all four, every time, not just the number on the bag.

quick_check.q: What does the "L" in the TILE manual handling framework stand for, and what does it cover?
quick_check.a: Load --- the weight, size, shape, and stability of the object being handled, including whether its contents could shift.

how_tested: expect questions asking you to identify the four TILE factors, or testing whether you know there is no fixed universal safe lifting weight.

title: Welfare Facilities Requirements
exam_alert: Welfare facilities aren't a fixed, one-size-fits-all checklist --- CDM 2015 requires them to match the size of the site and the specific hazards present.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes assume basic toilets and drinking water satisfy the full legal requirement. Showers specifically may be required where hazards such as cement or lead are present.
memory_aid: Toilets, washing, water, rest, and a place to change --- five categories, scaled to the site.

quick_check.q: Why might showers specifically be required on a site, beyond standard washing facilities?
quick_check.a: Because certain hazards, such as cement, lead, or biological agents, need to be washed off the skin promptly, which standard washbasins alone may not achieve.

how_tested: questions here often test whether you know facilities scale to the site's size and hazards, rather than a single fixed checklist applying identically everywhere.

title: Mental Health and Wellbeing on Site
exam_alert: Mental health sits inside the same general duty of care as physical safety --- not as a separate, lesser concern.
common_mistake: Some candidates treat mental health as outside the scope of health and safety entirely. It falls within the same employer duty of care as physical risk.
memory_aid: The duty of care doesn't stop at the skin --- it covers what's going on underneath it too.
how_tested: the test may present a colleague showing signs of struggling and ask for the appropriate response --- the correct answer is to check in or signpost support, not to do nothing because it feels like someone else's business.

title: Skin Health and Dermatitis Prevention
exam_alert: Wet cement causes genuine chemical burns through prolonged skin contact --- this is a real injury, not minor irritation, and the test treats it accordingly.
common_mistake: Cement-related skin damage is sometimes dismissed as "a bit of dryness." Left untreated, prolonged contact causes real burns and can lead to lasting dermatitis.
memory_aid: Wet cement doesn't just get you dirty --- it can burn you, and you might not feel it happening.

quick_check.q: Why is prolonged skin contact with wet cement a serious hazard rather than a minor irritation?
quick_check.a: Wet cement is highly alkaline, and prolonged contact can cause genuine chemical burns, often without the worker feeling significant pain at the time.

how_tested: expect questions testing whether you understand wet cement causes real chemical burns, and what prevents it, rather than treating it as routine mess to clean off later.

title: Sun Exposure and Heat Stress
exam_alert: Confusion or collapse in hot conditions is treated as heat stroke --- a medical emergency requiring immediate help, not a case of simply cooling down in your own time.
common_mistake: Sun exposure risk is sometimes dismissed because the damage isn't visible immediately. UV damage accumulates over years of outdoor work, not just from one occasion.
memory_aid: Thirsty already means you're behind --- drink on a schedule, not just when you notice you need to.
how_tested: the test often distinguishes general tiredness from the specific warning signs of heat stress, and tests the correct response once those signs appear.

title: Substance Misuse and Fitness for Work
exam_alert: Fitness for work covers legal, prescribed medication as much as alcohol or illegal drugs --- if it affects safe working, it must be disclosed.
common_mistake: Some candidates assume only obvious drunkenness counts as being unfit for work. Subtle impairment from medication or fatigue falls under the same duty to disclose and act on.
memory_aid: If it could slow your reactions or cloud your judgement, it's relevant to fitness for work --- whatever the label on the bottle says.

quick_check.q: What should a worker do if they believe a colleague may be unfit for work due to substance use or impairment?
quick_check.a: Report it to a supervisor rather than ignoring it, since an impaired colleague is a safety risk to themselves and everyone working around them.

how_tested: expect questions testing whether you know fitness for work covers legal medication, not only alcohol or illegal substances, and what the correct response is if a colleague appears impaired.

title: PPE: Legal Duties, Cost, and the Hierarchy of Control
exam_alert: PPE sits at the bottom of the hierarchy of control. It's used only for risks that remain after other, more effective controls have already been applied.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes think workers can be asked to pay for or contribute toward their own PPE. The employer must provide and maintain it free of charge.
memory_aid: PPE protects the person, but it's always the employer's wallet that pays.

quick_check.q: Where does PPE sit in the hierarchy of control, and who pays for it?
quick_check.a: PPE is the last resort, used only for risks remaining after other controls are applied, and the employer must always pay for it, including repairs and replacements.

how_tested: expect questions testing both the hierarchy --- PPE as a last resort, not a first response --- and the fact that the employer always bears the cost.

title: Head, Eye, and Foot Protection
exam_alert: A hard hat that's taken an impact is replaced even without visible damage --- the protective structure can fail invisibly.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes treat all eye protection as interchangeable. Goggles, glasses, and face shields each suit a different hazard --- fine dust, general impact, or flying debris.
memory_aid: If it's been hit, heated, or left in the sun, it's no longer trustworthy --- hard hats don't get second chances.

quick_check.q: Why should a hard hat be replaced after an impact, even with no visible crack?
quick_check.a: Because the protective shell can be structurally weakened internally in a way that isn't visible from the outside, so it can no longer be relied on.

how_tested: the test may ask why a hard hat with no visible damage is still replaced after an impact, or which eye protection matches a specific task such as grinding.

title: Hand Protection, Hearing Protection, and Hi-Vis Clothing
exam_alert: Gloves are removed near rotating machinery --- the entanglement risk they create outweighs the protection they offer in that specific situation.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes assume combining earplugs and earmuffs always gives better protection. Over-protection can block a worker from hearing alarms or shouted warnings when it isn't actually required.
memory_aid: Match the glove to the hazard, and take it off before the hazard becomes the glove itself.

quick_check.q: Why might a worker be told to remove gloves before working near rotating machinery?
quick_check.a: Because loose glove material can catch in the moving parts and drag the hand into the machinery, turning the glove itself into the hazard.

how_tested: expect questions on matching glove type to hazard, the rotating-machinery exception, and why hearing protection is a risk-assessed choice rather than always wearing maximum protection.

title: Respiratory Protective Equipment: Types, Fit, and Maintenance
exam_alert: Facial hair along a tight-fitting mask's seal line breaks the seal --- a worker in that situation needs a refit test or RPE that doesn't rely on a seal at all.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes assume a face-fit test only needs to happen once, ever. A refit is required whenever facial features change enough to affect the seal.
memory_aid: No seal, no protection --- anything that changes your face can change the fit.
how_tested: the test may describe a change to a worker's face --- weight change, facial hair, dental work --- and ask what should happen to their RPE as a result.

title: Safety Signage: Shapes, Colours, and Meanings
exam_alert: Shape is tested as rigorously as colour --- a mandatory sign is always a circle, a warning sign is always a triangle, whatever the specific instruction shown.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes mix up the two circular categories. Mandatory (blue, instructing) and prohibition (red, forbidding, with a diagonal line) are both circles but mean opposite things.
memory_aid: Red circle says stop, blue circle says do, yellow triangle says take care, green means the way out, red square means the way to fight a fire.

quick_check.q: Why does a safety sign's shape matter as much as its colour?
quick_check.a: Because shape lets a colour-blind worker, or a worker in poor light, still recognise a sign's meaning from its outline alone, without relying on colour perception.

how_tested: expect questions that show a sign's shape and colour and ask which category it belongs to, or ask what shape or colour a specific category uses.

title: The Work at Height Regulations 2005: Hierarchy and Duties
exam_alert: The hierarchy is strict and sequential --- avoid, then prevent, then minimise. A harness is the last resort, not the default first answer.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes jump straight to fall arrest equipment as the answer. Avoiding the work at height entirely, or preventing the fall with guardrails, comes first.
memory_aid: Avoid, prevent, minimise --- work from the ground up, not the harness down.

quick_check.q: What is the first question to ask under the Work at Height Regulations 2005, before any equipment is chosen?
quick_check.a: Whether the work at height can be avoided altogether, For example by doing the task from ground level instead.

how_tested: the test often presents a work-at-height scenario and asks which control should be considered first --- the correct answer works through avoid, then prevent, then minimise, in that order.

title: Ladders and Stepladders: Safe Use
exam_alert: Footing a ladder is the last resort for securing it, used only when tying, a stability device, and wedging are all impractical --- not the default method.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes treat ladders as suitable for any task. They're only appropriate for low-risk, short-duration work where a risk assessment supports their use.
memory_aid: One in four, hand and two, footing's the last thing you do.

quick_check.q: What does the 1 in 4 rule mean for positioning a leaning ladder?
quick_check.a: The base of the ladder sits one unit away from the wall for every four units of working height, giving roughly a 75-degree angle.

how_tested: expect questions on calculating or recognising the 1 in 4 rule, the correct order of methods to secure a ladder, and when a stepladder's two-feet-on-one-step rule applies for brief two-handed work.

title: Scaffolding: Erection, Inspection, and Safe Use
exam_alert: 7 days is a maximum interval, not a guideline --- and bad weather or alteration triggers an extra inspection regardless of when the last one happened.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes assume a scaffold inspected once when erected remains safe indefinitely. Conditions change, and regular reinspection is a legal requirement.
memory_aid: Before first use, every 7, and after the weather gets rough.

quick_check.q: Why does a scaffold need a competent person to inspect it every 7 days, not just once when first erected?
quick_check.a: Because conditions such as weather, ground movement, or site activity can cause a scaffold to deteriorate after erection, so regular reinspection confirms it's still safe to use.

how_tested: the test often asks for the maximum interval between scaffold inspections, or what triggers an inspection outside that routine schedule.

title: Edge Protection, Fall Restraint, and Fall Arrest
exam_alert: Fall arrest requires a rescue plan in addition to the equipment itself, because a worker suspended after a fall is at risk of suspension trauma if left too long.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes treat restraint and arrest as interchangeable terms for 'wearing a harness.' Restraint stops a fall from happening; arrest only catches one that's already started.
memory_aid: Restraint stops you reaching the edge. Arrest catches you after you've gone over it.

quick_check.q: What is the key difference between a fall restraint system and a fall arrest system?
quick_check.a: Restraint physically prevents a worker from reaching a fall hazard at all, while arrest catches a worker after a fall has already begun and requires a rescue plan.

how_tested: the test may describe a harness setup and ask whether it's restraint or arrest, based on whether the worker can reach the fall hazard at all.

title: MEWPs and Fragile Roofs
exam_alert: A fragile roof can give way without warning regardless of how solid it looks --- crawling boards, staging, and edge protection are used whatever the surface appears to be.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes assume a solid-looking roof surface is safe to walk on directly. Fragility isn't always visible, and the correct response is the same whatever it looks like.
memory_aid: If it says fragile, don't trust your feet --- trust the boards instead.

quick_check.q: Why should a worker never step directly onto a fragile roof surface, even if it looks solid?
quick_check.a: Because fragile roofing material can give way suddenly without warning regardless of its appearance, so access must spread the load using boards or staging instead.

how_tested: expect a scenario describing a roof that looks solid, testing whether you know appearance alone is never a safe basis for deciding a surface will bear weight.

title: Excavations: Collapse Risk and Temporary Support
exam_alert: A competent person must inspect an excavation at the start of every shift, and again after any event --- such as heavy rain or a fall of material --- that could have affected its stability.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes assume an excavation inspected once at the start of a job remains safe throughout. It needs reinspection at the start of each shift and after anything that could affect stability.
memory_aid: No ground is trustworthy on its own --- batter it back or box it in, every shift, no exceptions.

quick_check.q: How often must a competent person inspect an open excavation while work is ongoing?
quick_check.a: At the start of every shift, and again after any event --- such as heavy rain or a fall of material --- that could have affected its stability.

how_tested: the test often asks what must happen before excavation work begins, or how often an open excavation must be inspected while work continues.

title: Avoiding Underground and Overhead Services
exam_alert: Underground services must be identified and marked before excavation starts --- not discovered by striking them during digging.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes think overhead power line danger requires actual contact. Getting close enough can cause a flashover without the plant touching the line at all.
memory_aid: Scan before you dig, and keep your distance overhead --- contact isn't the only way power lines hurt you.
how_tested: expect questions on what must be done before excavating to avoid underground services, and how overhead line risk is managed when work beneath a line can't be avoided.

title: Confined Spaces: Recognition and the Duty to Avoid Entry
exam_alert: Avoiding entry altogether is the first duty under the Confined Spaces Regulations --- not how to enter safely, but whether entry is needed at all.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes list only toxic atmosphere as a confined space risk. Oxygen deficiency or enrichment, a flammable atmosphere, and engulfment are equally recognised dangers.
memory_aid: Air, fire, and being buried alive --- a confined space can kill you four different ways before you've done any work.

quick_check.q: What is the first question to ask when work involves a confined space?
quick_check.a: Whether the work can be done without anyone entering the space at all, For example using remote cameras or tools operated from outside.

how_tested: the test may ask what must be considered first when work involves a confined space --- the correct answer is always whether entry can be avoided altogether.

title: Confined Spaces: Permits, Gas Testing, and Rescue
exam_alert: Rescue arrangements must be fully in place before anyone enters a confined space --- they are never something to arrange once a problem has already occurred.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes assume adding oxygen to a stale confined space makes it safer to breathe. It instead sharply increases the risk of fire or explosion and must never be done.
memory_aid: If the rescue plan isn't ready, nobody goes in --- not even for a minute.

quick_check.q: Why must oxygen never be used to 'sweeten' the air in a confined space before entry?
quick_check.a: Adding oxygen raises its concentration well above normal, which sharply increases the risk of fire or explosion rather than making the space safer to breathe.

how_tested: expect questions testing whether rescue arrangements must be ready before entry, and why oxygen is never added to a confined space's atmosphere.

title: Electrical Safety on Site: Voltage, RCDs, and Inspection
exam_alert: 110V plugs and connectors are always yellow --- recognising this colour coding is directly testable and prevents the wrong supply being used.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes think an RCD alone makes 230V equipment as safe as 110V. The two work together: lower voltage limits how severe a shock is, and the RCD limits how long it lasts --- neither replaces the other.
memory_aid: Battery beats yellow, yellow beats blue --- and whichever one you use, check it before you plug it in.

quick_check.q: Why is 110V reduced voltage preferred over 230V mains for corded power tools on site?
quick_check.a: Its earthed centre-tapped transformer means each live conductor is only around 55V to earth, so a shock at that level is far less likely to be fatal than one from full 230V mains.

how_tested: expect questions on what colour a 110V plug is, why 110V is safer than 230V, and what an RCD actually does.

title: Plant and Vehicle Safety: Competence and Pre-Use Checks
exam_alert: Operating plant always requires training and competence specific to that machine --- experience with similar equipment, or general confidence, isn't a substitute.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes assume a vehicle that looks fine doesn't need its daily check. The check is required every shift regardless of how the machine appears.
memory_aid: Looks fine isn't the same as checked and signed --- do the check every shift, no exceptions.

quick_check.q: What should an operator do if a pre-use check reveals a fault, such as a hydraulic leak?
quick_check.a: Report it and take the machine out of use rather than continuing to operate it until the fault is corrected.

how_tested: the test may describe a worker using plant without the right card or certification, or skipping a pre-use check, and ask what should happen instead.

title: Site Traffic Management: Segregation, Routes, and Reversing
exam_alert: Segregating pedestrians and vehicles with separate routes is more effective than relying on a banksman, and removing the need to reverse (such as with a one-way system) comes before minimising or managing it.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes treat a banksman as the primary control for reversing risk. A banksman is used only once removing or minimising the need to reverse isn't practicable.
memory_aid: Separate first, remove the reverse second, and a banksman only once the first two run out.
how_tested: expect questions on what the most effective control for pedestrian-vehicle risk is, and where a banksman sits in that hierarchy relative to segregation and removing the need to reverse.

title: Banksmen and Signallers: Roles and Safe Communication
exam_alert: Losing visual contact with a banksman or signaller means stopping immediately --- not slowing down, not continuing carefully, but a full stop.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes assume a radio link is enough without visual contact. Visibility between driver and banksman or signaller is the rule the whole system depends on.
memory_aid: Can't see them, can't move --- visual contact is the whole deal, not a nice-to-have.

quick_check.q: What must a driver or crane operator do if they lose sight of the banksman or signaller directing them?
quick_check.a: Stop immediately, rather than continuing cautiously based on the last signal given.

how_tested: the test may describe a banksman or signaller going out of view and ask what the driver or operator should do --- the correct answer is always to stop immediately.

title: LOLER: Lifting Plans and the Appointed Person
exam_alert: The appointed person's competence must be specific to the type of lift being planned --- general lifting experience alone isn't enough for an unusual or complex operation.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes assume every single lift needs its own formal written plan. Routine lifts following an established, proven procedure may not, but anything that departs from standard practice does.
memory_aid: Routine lifts follow the procedure; unusual lifts get their own plan, written by someone who actually understands that specific lift.

quick_check.q: Why must the appointed person planning a lift have knowledge specific to that type of lift, not just general lifting experience?
quick_check.a: Different lifts carry different risks from load geometry, surroundings, and equipment, so the plan only properly controls those risks if the planner understands the specific lift, not lifting in general.

how_tested: expect questions on who is responsible for planning a lift, and what distinguishes a lift that needs a full written plan from one that doesn't.

title: Thorough Examination, Lifting Accessories, and Safe Working Load
exam_alert: Equipment used to lift people, and lifting accessories such as slings, are examined every 6 months --- not the general 12-month interval that applies to other lifting equipment.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes assume all lifting equipment follows the same 12-month examination cycle. Equipment lifting people and accessories like slings are examined twice as often.
memory_aid: People and accessories: every 6. Everything else: every 12.
how_tested: the test often asks for the specific examination interval for equipment used to lift people, or for lifting accessories, which is shorter than the general 12-month interval.

title: The Waste Hierarchy and Duty of Care
exam_alert: Prevention or reduction of waste is always the top priority in the hierarchy --- not recycling, which many candidates assume comes first.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes treat disposal as a neutral, default option. It's the least preferred choice in the hierarchy, used only once every other option has been ruled out.
memory_aid: Prevent, reuse, recycle, recover, dispose --- in that order, every time.

quick_check.q: What is the single highest priority in the waste hierarchy?
quick_check.a: Preventing or reducing waste in the first place, considered as early as the design and pre-construction stage.

how_tested: the test often asks which option in the waste hierarchy comes first, expecting prevention or reduction rather than recycling.

title: Waste Transfer and Hazardous Waste Documentation
exam_alert: Hazardous waste always needs a consignment note in addition to the standard waste transfer note --- the transfer note alone isn't sufficient.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes assume responsibility for waste ends once a skip leaves site. The duty of care continues until the waste reaches an authorised destination.
memory_aid: Ordinary waste gets a transfer note. Hazardous waste gets that note plus a consignment note --- never just one.
how_tested: expect questions on what extra documentation hazardous waste requires beyond the standard transfer note, and who is responsible for checking a waste carrier is properly licensed.

title: Preventing Water and Land Pollution: Bunding and Spill Response
exam_alert: A bund must hold 110% of the largest single container stored within it --- not 110% of everything combined, and not just the volume of what's normally kept there.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes assume a bund just needs to match the total combined volume of everything stored inside it. It's measured against the single largest container, with a margin above that.
memory_aid: 110% of the biggest one --- not the total, just the largest single container it has to outlast.

quick_check.q: Why must rainwater collecting in a bund never be allowed to build up unchecked?
quick_check.a: It reduces the bund's spare capacity to contain a spill, and if it needs removing, it may itself count as contaminated waste requiring proper disposal.

how_tested: the test often states a percentage figure for bund capacity and asks whether it meets the legal minimum, or asks what a bund's capacity is measured against.

title: Noise, Dust, and Nuisance Control
exam_alert: Noise and dust nuisance control protects people beyond the site boundary and applies even when on-site exposure limits are already being met.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes assume noise and dust control is only about worker exposure limits covered elsewhere in this guide. Nuisance to neighbours is a distinct, additional duty.
memory_aid: Protecting your own workers isn't the same as protecting the street outside the fence --- both duties apply, separately.

quick_check.q: Why might a site need to control dust even when levels are already safe for the workers on site?
quick_check.a: Because noise and dust nuisance control is a separate duty aimed at protecting neighbouring properties and the public, independent of whether worker exposure limits are being met.

how_tested: expect a question distinguishing nuisance control, which protects neighbours and the public, from the exposure controls in Chapter 4, which protect workers on site.

title: Protecting Wildlife and Habitats
exam_alert: There's no single safe calendar date for clearing vegetation without a nesting check --- breeding season timing varies, so a check is the correct approach regardless of the date.
common_mistake: Candidates sometimes assume clearance outside the 'usual' nesting months is automatically risk-free. Timing varies enough that a check is still the right response.
memory_aid: No safe date, only a safe check --- look before you clear, whatever month it is.

quick_check.q: What should a site do if an active bird's nest is found during a pre-clearance check?
quick_check.a: Leave it undisturbed, set up a temporary exclusion zone around it, and continue clearance elsewhere until the young have fledged.

how_tested: the test may describe vegetation clearance taking place at a particular time of year and ask whether a nesting check is still needed --- the correct answer is almost always yes, because there's no fixed safe date.
